Mechanics' Bank of Alexandria v. Withers
“But this act, affirming a pre-existing power, ought not to be construed to vary the nature of that power, unless words are employed which manifest *109 such intention.”

"This court has been often called upon to consider the sixteenth section of the judiciary act of 1789, and as often, either expressly or by the course of its decisions, has held, that it is merely declaratory, making no alteration whatever in the rules of equity on the subject of legal remedy."

"the thirty-fourth section of the Judiciary Act of the United States; in which it is enacted that the laws of the several states shall be rules of decision in the courts of the United States; and which has been uniformly held to be no more than a declaration of what the law would have been without it"
Edward Bradford, in Error v. Robert W. Williams, and John Judge, in Error v. Robert W. Williams
"and is, indeed, only declaratory of what would have been die legal effect, without the particular phraseology of the section."

Parker v. Winnipiseogee Lake Cotton & Woollen Co.
"This is merely declaratory of the pre-existing rule,"

"The sixteenth section of the Judiciary Act of 1789, enacting 'that suits in equity shall not be sustained in either of the courts of the United States in any case where plain, adequate, and complete remedy may be had at law,' is merely declaratory and made no change in the pre-existing law."
"so far as it 'gives authority to the President, it is simply declaratory of the long-established law.'"

“The provision may be used in aid of construction if there is doubt, but not as an affirmative grant of a positive right.”

"these were drawn from the statute 7 Anne, c. 12, which was declaratory simply of the law of nations, which Lord Mansfield observed, in Heathfield v. Chilton, 4 Burrow, 2015, 2016, the act did not intend to alter and could not alter."
